title: Study on the improving effect of Nb-V microalloying on the hydrogen induced delayed fracture property of 22MnB5 press hardened steel
abstract: Press-hardened steel (PHS) is widely used in manufacturing automobile parts and is sensitive to hydrogen embrittlement (HE). A novel 0.04Nb-0.04 V (wt%) PHS (22MnB5NbV) was developed based on 22MnB5. The constant-strain bending test shows the duration of no-cracking for 22MnB5NbV in 0.5 mol/L HCl is > 300 h even though the pre-bending stress is 1500–1600 MPa, and that for 22MnB5 is 12 h. The prior austenite grain size and martensite lath width in 22MnB5NbV decrease from 13.4 to 8.2 μm and from 0.35 to 0.15 μm due to Nb-V microalloying, respectively, resulting in the hydrogen trapped in reversible hydrogen traps increases by 2.09 times according to thermal desorption spectrometry analysis. The leaching experiment presents that 88% Nb and 25% V exist in the form of precipitates rather than in solution in 22MnB5NbV. The nano-precipitates (< 10 nm) are mainly (Nb, Ti, V)C, in which Nb-bearing precipitates account for the largest proportion and supply the heterogeneous nucleation sites for V-bearing precipitates, this is confirmed by atom probe tomography (APT). APT confirms that the hydrogen is mainly trapped at the interface of Fe matrix/carbide. The dispersed nano-carbide and refined microstructure resulting from the Nb-V microalloying are the key factors improving the HE of 22MnB5NbV.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Automotive exhaust is one of the primary pollution sources across the world. To save energy and reduce emissions, the automobile lightweight is greatly proposed in these years  [1–3] . The ultra-high strength steels (UHSS) which can decrease the total weight of an automobile in the case of achieving a similar collision property have been widely concerned and applied. Among them, the boron-alloyed martensitic press-hardened steels (PHS) are commonly used to produce the safety anti-intrusion parts and structural reinforcements of vehicles such as door beams, impact beams, bumpers, A-pillars, and B-pillars. The ultimate tensile strength for PHS is usually > 1500 MPa and even up to 2000 MPa  [4] . Although the PHS has excellent mechanical properties, it is normally accompanied by other application problems, such as low toughness and hydrogen embrittlement (HE). The HE is a common phenomenon due to the matrix microstructure of PHS is mainly lath martensite with a high density of dislocation, leading to a quite low critical hydrogen concentration for HE during hot forming and automotive service, especially as the strength of the PHS is > 1200 MPa  [5,6] . Hence, how to improve the resistance to HE of PHS attracts great attention.

Although there are many studies on HE, there is still a lack of a universal HE theory  [7,8] . The existing HE theory mainly includes the hydrogen pressure theory  [9] , hydrogen-enhanced decohesion mechanism (HEDE)  [10] , hydrogen-enhanced local plasticity mechanism (HELP)  [11] , hydrogen-enhanced strain-induced vacancy mechanism (HESIV)  [12] , Microvoid coalescence mechanism (MVC)  [13] , etc  [14] . In 1941, Zapffe and Sims  [9]  proposed the hydrogen pressure theory and pointed out that the diffusion and aggregation of hydrogen atoms in the internal defects of metals would lead to the generation of the hydrogen molecule and increase the local hydrogen gas pressure, and eventually resulting in cracking or hydrogen-induced bubbles  [15] . The hydrogen pressure theory only considers the loading effect of hydrogen pressure, but without considering the embrittlement effect of diffusing hydrogen so that the actual hydrogen pressure is much lower than the theoretically predicted critical hydrogen pressure for hydrogen-induced fracture  [16] . In 1926, Pfeil  [10]  developed the HEDE mechanism and stated that the hydrogen could reduce the cohesive strength of interatomic, resulting in the atomic separation occurring with a lower tensile stress. The HEDE mechanism is supported by the observation of cleavage-like fracture, but it is mainly aimed at transition metals and has not been directly demonstrated by measuring the cohesive force  [17] . In 1972, Beachem  [11]  proposed the HELP mechanism through the observation of the tear ridges on the hydrogen induced brittle fracture surfaces. This mechanism suggested that hydrogen can reduce the critical stress for dislocation emission and enhance the mobility of dislocation. In addition, the dislocation motion can be the carrier of hydrogen diffusion, resulting in the formation of a hydrogen atmosphere like the Cottrell carbon atmosphere  [18] . The dislocation and hydrogen will accumulate in a local region under sustained stress and finally cause local plastic deformation  [19] . The HELP mechanism mainly focuses attention on the interaction between hydrogen and dislocation and is utilized to reveal the fracture surface with a dimple in hydrogenated alloys. But there are still some phenomena that conflict with the HELP mechanism, such as the macroscopic tensile tests presented that the dislocation motion was suppressed by hydrogen in IN718 alloys  [20] . In 2004, Nagumo  [12]  assumed that hydrogen accelerated the formation of strain-induced vacancies, which contributed to the void initiation and fracture of alloys. This is the HESIV mechanism and is confirmed by simulations  [21] . In 2012, Neeraj et al.  [13]  proposed the MVC mechanism based on the hydrogen induced ductile fracture with a shear ligament. This mechanism explained that the ductile process happened in several stages (void nucleation, void growth, void coalescence, and crack extension). Li et al.  [7]  pointed out the essence of MVC mechanism is the comprehensive effects of the HELP, HEDE, and HESIV mechanisms. It should be noted that the above HE theories are mainly based on the postmortem observation and analysis of the dislocation and fracture characteristics of hydrogen-induced cracks. The dynamic evolutions of the diffusion and accumulation of hydrogens, the slip and pile-up of dislocations, and the origin and propagation of micro-crack, which involved hydrogen-induced fracture, are still not well directly confirmed experimentally at an atomic scale. Moreover, it is difficult to reveal all the HE phenomena with only one mechanism, sometimes several mechanisms act simultaneously, and it is related to the material category. For most steels, the HELP and HEDE mechanisms are generally acceptable.

The in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observation and atomic simulations realized that the dislocation mobility in the presence of hydrogen is the key factor inducing HE  [22,23] . Strong evidence demonstrated that the origin of HE is due to the interaction between the diffusible hydrogen atom and dislocation  [24] . Therefore, lightening or inhibiting the accumulation of diffusible hydrogen at dislocation or reducing the inhalation of diffusible hydrogen during the process of production, processing, and service of steel is an effective way to anti-HE. Here, we mainly focus on the HE of uncoated PHS. The hydrogen origin mainly comes from the production process but does not involve the service process. Usually, there is little difference in hydrogen inhalation for PHS as compared with conventional steel during the production process of smelting, continuous casting, pickling, heat treatment, etc. Although vacuum desorption and atmosphere protection can reduce the entry of hydrogen, the inhalation of hydrogen cannot be avoided completely. Thus, hindering the free diffusion and abnormal accumulation of hydrogen in PHS is also important to improve HE. It has been proved that the nanoscale carbides have a higher hydrogen desorption activation energy and are usually classified as an irreversible hydrogen trap  [7,25–27] . Normally, the hydrogen atoms are trapped in the stress field surrounding the interface of Fe matrix/precipitates  [28] . Wei et al.  [29]  pointed out that the capacity of hydrogen trapping by the (semi)coherent carbides varied in the descending order of NbC > TiC > VC based on thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) analysis.

Since the nanoscale carbide can efficiently trap hydrogen, it is favorable to improve the HE of steel by microalloying. There are several benefits to microalloying. Firstly, the nanoscale precipitates which are strong hydrogen trapping sites can inhibit the hydrogen motion, resulting in a decrease in the content of diffusible hydrogens  [27] . Secondly, the hydrogens will distribute more uniformly based on the fact that the nanoscale precipitates are usually dispersed in steel, which will reduce the probability of the local accumulation of hydrogens  [30] . Finally, the microstructure usually can be refined due to microalloying. Although the grain boundaries are reversible hydrogen trapping sites, a finer microstructure can also divide the hydrogens more uniformly  [31] . So, increasing the amount of nano-precipitates and refining the microstructure by microalloying is an effective method to abate the hydrogen-dislocation interaction and improve the HE of steels, which has been well accepted  [27,31–33] . The improving effect of Nb or V microalloying on the HE of PHS was widely studied in recent years. Lin et al.  [5]  pointed out that the addition of Nb in 22MnB5 (PHS) could reduce hydrogen diffusivity so that improving HE. Zhang et al.  [32]  found the main reason for improving the HE of Nb microalloyed 22MnB5 was the hydrogen trapping effect of NbC and the grain refinement induced by Nb(C, N). Liu et al.  [34]  suggested that grain refinement and the dissolved Nb, which may act as shallow hydrogen traps, could improve the HE of high-strength martensitic steel. Fan et al.  [30]  speculated that the highly dispersed nanoscale NbC precipitates could hinder the accumulation of hydrogen at the potential crack nucleation sites of high-strength low-alloy steel. For V microalloying, Cho et al.  [27]  proposed the addition of V in aluminized PHS increased the capacity of hydrogen adsorption due to an increased density of hydrogen traps (VC precipitates). Chen et al.  [31]  stated that an apparent lower diffusion coefficient of hydrogen was obtained due to the addition of 0.14 wt% V into 30MnB5 (PHS). Asahi et al.  [35]  found the de-trapping of hydrogen was very slow while the trapping presumably proceeds rapidly for the PHS containing VC precipitates. In addition to PHS, V additions could also improve the HE of X80 pipeline steel  [36] , 0.6 wt% C tempered martensitic steel  [37] , and high-strength bolt steel  [38] . In particular, Chen et al.  [39]  and Takahashi et al.  [28]  confirmed that the hydrogen atoms were trapped at the interface of NbC/Fe and the C vacancy on the surface of VC using APT. Although the improving effect of Nb or V microalloying on the HE of PHS is verified, whether the Nb or V has a better effect on improving HE is still difficult to conclude. Besides, Zhang et al.  [40]  pointed out that the combined addition of Nb-V in spring steel exhibited an excellent fracture strength for the SSRT specimen with pre-charged hydrogen. Wang et al.  [41]  suggested the tensile strength of high-strength TRIP steel microalloyed by Nb-V was satisfactory, resulting from the fine and dispersed (Nb, V)C. Jana et al.  [42]  indicated that the C-Mn-Cr steel (0.15–0.22 wt% C) with 0.11V–0.034Nb (in wt%) presented a greater improving effect in strength due to finer precipitates. These studies suggest that the combined addition of Nb-V in steel could get excellent performance in some respects. Thus, we speculated whether there is an excellent performance in anti-HE for the PHS microalloyed with combined Nb-V.

In the present study, more attention was paid to the improving effect of Nb-V combined microalloying on the HE of PHS. A novel PHS with 0.04Nb–0.04V (in wt%) was developed based on the traditional PHS of 22MnB5. The constant strain bending test in an acidic environment and slow strain rate test (SSRT) were applied to evaluate the HE property, and TDS analysis was employed to quantify the capacity of hydrogen trapping. The fracture surface morphology, microstructure, and precipitates were characterized using an optical microscope (OM), scanning electron microscope (SEM) with electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD), and TEM, respectively. The precipitation behavior of Nb-V bearing precipitates was estimated by JmatPro 10.0 (developed by Sente Software Ltd.) and the leaching experiment. Especially, the morphology of nanoscale precipitate with a compound composition of Nb, V, and C, as well as the spatial distribution of the hydrogen at the interface of Fe matrix/carbide was identified using APT. The effect of Nb-V combined microalloying on the precipitation of nanoscale carbides and the capacity of hydrogen trapping were explored.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The novel Nb-V microalloyed PHS (22MnB5NbV) was designed based on the conventional PHS of 22MnB5, in which 0.04Nb and 0.04V (in wt%) were added in the form of ferroniobium and ferrovanadium during the process of LF refining. The chemical compositions of the 22MnB5 are 0.24C, 0.24Si, 1.32Mn, 0.011P, 0.0032N, 0.031Al, 0.13Cr, 0.0021B, 0.031Ti, and Fe balance (in wt%). The raw material was prepared by Maanshan Iron & Steel Co., Ltd. First, the continuous casting billet was hot-rolled to 4–5 mm (thickness) through eight passes, and the temperature range was 1050–900 °C. Then, it was cold-rolled to 1.5 mm (thickness) through six passes at room temperature. For continuous annealing, the rolled plate was firstly held at 800 °C for 270 s and then cooled to 680 °C in the furnace, followed by roller cooling to 400 °C. The final matrix phases were mainly ferrite and pearlite. The hot stamping process was carried out as follows: the steel plate was held at 930 °C for 280 s in the arc electric furnace with an inert nitrogen atmosphere, and then it was transferred into a flat die for quenching with a cooling rate of 40 °C/s.

sections.heading: Experimental procedures
paragraphs:
Experiment I: constant strain bending test. The pre-bending specimen immersed in the 0.5 mol/L hydrochloric acid solution was applied to assess the HE sensitivity of the PHS, according to the standard of T/CSAE 155–2020. The strain at the bending apex of the specimen, which was adjusted via the pressure from the screws at the two endpoints of the fixture, was measured using a strain gauge. The corresponding stress was obtained from the engineering strain–stress curve measured in advance. The drawing of the bending specimens as well as the schematic illustration of the HE experiments are shown in  Fig. 1 
                         (a) and (b). The initial span between the two endpoints of the specimen without pre-bending is 150 mm, and the spans for the specimens with 1100–1600 MPa pre-stress at the bending apex are in the range of 145–80 mm. The higher the pre-stress at the bending apex, the smaller the span. The qualified duration of no cracking for the constant strain bending test was 100 h in previous works  [32]  while that was 300 h in the present study. The constant strain bending test was repeated five times under the same bending condition.

Experiment II: SSRT. The dimension of the specimen for SSRT (uniaxial tensile test) is shown in  Fig. 1 (c). The specimens were ground using SiC sandpaper up to 2000 grit and cleaned with ethanol. Then the SSRT was performed at room temperature using a 50 kN SSRT system, as shown in  Fig. 1 (d). To evaluate the effect of tiny amounts of hydrogen (< 0.1 ppm) penetration on the HE of the novel Nb-V PHS, the specimens were not hydrogen pre-charging but immersed in a 0.2 mol·L -1  NaOH solution at a current density of 3.6 mA/cm 2  for electrochemical continuous hydrogen charging during SSRT, as shown in  Fig. 1 (e). The SSRT was performed at a cross head displacement speed of 0.015 mm/min, corresponding to a strain rate of 1.56 × 10 -5  s −1 . The SSRT was repeated three times for each case. It should be noted that it is hard to equip an extensometer during the SSRT due to the existence of an electrochemical hydrogen charging tank, as shown in  Fig. 1 (d) and (e). In view of this, the gauge length of the test sample cannot be determined, resulting in the stress-displacement curve instead of the stress–strain curve can be obtained during SSRT. Thus, only the tensile strength but not the yield strength and elongation can be accurately gained from SSRT.

Experiment III: TDS. The hydrogen content in the specimens after the constant strain bending test was measured by TDS. The TDS spectras were obtained by heating the specimens (3 × 3 × 1.4, mm) from room temperature to 800 °C at a rate of 6.66 °C/min.

Experiment IV: leaching experiments. To quantify the content of Nb and V exist in the form of precipitates and solution, two pieces of polished specimens (22MnB5NbV, 40.8 and 51.9 mg) were put in the etching solutions of HNO 3 :HCl:HF (1:3:1) and pure HCl, respectively. The two etching solutions were designed to estimate the total and non-precipitated content of Nb (and V) in 22MnB5NbV, respectively.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs: The microstructure was characterized by a combination of OM, SEM-EBSD, TEM, and APT. An FEI Nova400 SEM was used for the SEM imaging and EBSD analyses at 20 kV. The EBSD specimens (5 × 5 × 1, mm) were first mechanically polished using SiC sandpaper with 400–3000 grit. Then the specimens were electropolished in 7% perchloric acid and 93% ethanol solution for 1 min to remove the surface deformation, and the current density of electropolish was 450 mA/cm 2 . The step size of SEM-EBSD observation was 0.1 μm. An FEI Tecnai G2 F20 transmission electron microscope with a 200 kV electron beam was used to investigate the martensitic lath structure and Nb-V precipitates. The TEM specimens were first mechanically polished and then prepared by ion milling.

An CAMECA LEAP 4000X HR using 40 pJ ultraviolet laser-pulsing was used to obtain high-resolution 3D atom maps of nanoscale carbide and hydrogen distribution. The preparation of APT specimens was similar to previous work  [33] . It must be noted that the method of electrochemical hydrogen (H) pre-charging was applied to detect the spatial distribution of hydrogen in Fe matrix and precipitates, as in the previous studies  [33,43] . But Chen et al.  [39]  and Takahashi et al.  [28]  pointed out that the naturally occurring hydrogen, which is primarily a contaminant, can be absorbed on the specimen during APT testing. To address this problem, the APT testing with deuterium (D) charging and cryogenic transfer was developed, in which deuterium-charging enables separation of the deuterium charged into the specimen from the background hydrogen and the cryogenic transfer is to prevent the charged deuterium from escaping  [44] . This modified APT testing is more advanced, but only a few institutions have mastered it in the world. Hence, we adopted the traditional method of charging hydrogen but not charging deuterium, as in the previous works  [33,43] .

sections.heading: HE property
paragraphs:
The mechanical properties of 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV before and after the hot stamping process are listed in  Table 1 
                         . Before hot stamping, the yield strength and tensile strength of 22MnB5NbV are slightly smaller than those of 22MnB5 while the elongation is the opposite. The difference in mechanical properties may be caused by the fact that the microstructure was not the same between 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, as in previous work  [5] . Moreover, the microstructures for the 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV before hot stamping are composed of ferrite and pearlite, in which the increasing effect of dissolved carbon (C) on the strength is greater than that of microstructure refinement and precipitates. The precipitation of (Nb, V)C in 22MnB5NbV has a small effect on the refinement of rolled microstructure (ferrite and pearlite) but can consume the dissolved C, resulting in the dissolved C content in 22MnB5NbV being lower than that in 22MnB5. Thus, the 22MnB5NbV shows a smaller yield strength and tensile strength. After hot stamping, the tensile strength is > 1600 MPa but the elongation decreases distinctly for both 22MnB5NbV and 22MnB5, indicating the presence of high-portion martensitic microstructure.

The duration of no cracking for the constant strain bending test under different pre-bending stress is listed in  Table 2 
                         . For 22MnB5, the duration of no cracking presents a remarkable decrease from > 300 h to < 100 h while the pre-bending stress is > 1400 MPa. In particular, it is only 12 h when the pre-bending stress is 1500–1600 MPa. In contrast, the 22MnB5NbV shows an excellent anti-HE property, in which the duration of no cracking is > 300 h even at 1500–1600 MPa. Previous studies suggested grain boundary and nanoscale carbide were hydrogen traps, which usually have a positive effect on improving HE  [39,45] .

sections.heading: Hydrogen adsorption capacity
paragraphs:
To investigate the origin of the HE resistance of the novel PHS, the capacity of hydrogen absorption in 22MnB5NbV and 22MnB5 was evaluated using TDS.  Fig. 2 
                          illustrates the TDS results for the specimens taken from the constant strain bending test with the pre-bending stress of 1500–1600 MPa. For both 22MnB5NbV and 22MnB5, two hydrogen desorption peaks are found at the temperature ranges of 100–300 °C and 350–550 °C, corresponding to the reversible (grain boundary/dislocation-type) and irreversible (nanoscale precipitates) hydrogen traps, respectively  [46] . The amount of desorbed hydrogen was measured by integrating the area beneath of the TDS curves in  Fig. 2 . Results show that the hydrogen trapped in the reversible sites are 0.0125 and 0.0261 ppm for 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, respectively. That is to say, the capacity of hydrogen absorption in reversible sites for 22MnB5NbV is 2 times that for 22MnB5. Meanwhile, the hydrogen trapped in the irreversible site is 0.0392 and 0.0487 ppm for 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, respectively, indicating that the 22MnB5NbV has a better performance in the capacity of hydrogen trapping than 22MnB5. This is due to the Nb-V microalloying which results in the refinement of microstructure and massive precipitation of nanoscale carbides in 22MnB5NbV. The difference in microstructure and nanoscale carbides between the two steels will be discussed later.

sections.heading: Tensile fracture morphology
paragraphs:
Fig. 3 
                          shows the SSRT curves for the 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV with and without H-charging. There is little difference in strength and ductility between 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV without H-charging. But under the condition of H-charging, the strength and ductility deteriorate significantly both for 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, and that for the 22MnB5NbV is slightly better than that for 22MnB5. The condition of H-charging is mild, and the tensile time is < 3 h for the SSRT with H-charging. Thus, the amount of H-charging is slight and unsaturated in both the 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV. In other words, the 22MnB5NbV does not play a full role in the adequate capacity of hydrogen trapping, resulting in little difference in anti-HE between 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV during SSRT. But it can be concluded that the mechanical properties of PHS have high sensitivity to hydrogen.

Fig. 4 
                          presents the fracture morphology of the SSRT specimens for the 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV with and without H-charging. The fracture surface contains ductile dimpled features in both 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV under the condition without H-charging, as shown in  Fig. 4 (a) and (b). But under the condition with H-charging, the 22MnB5 shows more quasi-cleavage and secondary crack while the 22MnB5NbV still presents the ductile feature with dimples, as shown in  Fig. 4 (c) and (d). This suggests that the 22MnB5NbV has a more satisfactory toughness than 22MnB5 in the presence of hydrogen, which corresponds to the excellent property of anti-HE for 22MnB5NbV.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs:
To investigate the difference in anti-HE between the 22MnB5NbV and 22MnB5, the microstructures were characterized.  Fig. 5 
                         ,  Fig. 6 
                         ,  Fig. 7 
                         , and  Fig. 8 
                          show the initial microstructure observed by OM, SEM-EBSD, and TEM, respectively. The prior austenite grain sizes (PAGS) for 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV are 13.4 and 8.2 μm, respectively, as shown in  Fig. 5 . The austenite grain refinement in 22MnB5NbV is mainly attributed to the pinning effect of (Ti, Nb)(C, N) on austenite growth and the finer grain is the main reason for the increased yield strength of 22MnB5NbV that after hot stamping, as listed in  Table 1 .

Fig. 6  presents the microstructure of the as-quenched specimens for 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV via SEM-EBSD. The red and black lines represent the low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs, ≤ 15°) and high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs, > 15°), respectively. Usually, the LAGBs are more beneficial for anti-HE  [33,47] . There is little difference in the relative frequency of the LAGBs between 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, and that is 33.42% and 30.49% for 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, respectively, as shown in  Fig. 6 (a-d). But the specific surface area of the LAGBs in 22MnB5NbV should be much more than that in 22MnB5 due to the finer microstructure, resulting in better performance in anti-HE.  Fig. 6 (e) and (f) intuitively present that there are many dislocations in intra-grain both for 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, and the dislocations are likely to be located at the boundaries of the martensite sub-structures, such as packet, block, and lath. The Kernel Average Misorientation (KAM) map indicates that the density of dislocation in 22MnB5 is a little greater than that in 22MnB5NbV, as shown in  Fig. 6 (g) and (h). The HELP mechanism suggests that the dislocation is the medium for the diffusion of hydrogen atoms under stress. A higher density of dislocation means a greater risk of hydrogen accumulation and hydrogen induced crack, illustrating that the HE sensitivity of 22MnB5 is stronger than that of 22MnB5NbV.

Fig. 7  presents the EBSD texture analysis for 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV. There seems little texture in both 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, illustrating that the Nb-V microalloying has a small effect on the texture. This means the texture may not play a role in improving the HE of 22MnB5NbV. The martensite lath in 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV was observed using TEM. The martensite lath width in 22MnB5NbV is 0.15 μm while that is 0.35 μm in 22MnB5, as shown in  Fig. 8 (a) and (b). In addition,  Fig. 8 (c) shows that there is a high density of dislocations located in the boundaries of martensite lath, corresponding to the KAM analysis.

The refined microstructure is an important factor that improves the resistance to HE because the grain boundary is in favor of hydrogen trapping  [37,46] . As the minimum unit in martensite, the apparent refinement of martensite lath in 22MnB5NbV can produce a much larger area of grain boundary that acts as hydrogen traps. This is the reason why the 22MnB5NbV traps a larger amount of hydrogen in the 22MnB5, as shown in  Fig. 2  (the 1st peak at 100–300 °C). In other words, the refinement of martensite lath caused by the Nb-V microalloying contributes to a certain proportion of the enhanced resistance to HE for 22MnB5NbV.

sections.heading: Nanoscale precipitates
paragraphs:
To evaluate the precipitation behavior of the Nb-bearing and V-bearing nanoscale second phase, the thermodynamics calculation was performed via JmatPro 10.0, in which the processing scheme of PHS was completely set to the same as the experiment, i.e., the austenitized and quenched processes were considered. The database of General Steel was selected.  Fig. 9 
                         (a) and (b) show the proportion of the elements in the precipitated phase of M(C, N).  Fig. 9 (a) indicates that a large number of Ti(C, N) precipitate above 900 °C, and Cr(C, N) starts to precipitate below 400 °C. The precipitates are dominated by (Ti, Cr)C, and the nitride is negligible in 22MnB5 due to the nitrogen content is much less than the carbon content. It can be found there are more types of carbide in 22MnB5NbV owing to the addition of Nb and V. NbC and TiC preferentially precipitate at the temperature above 900 °C, and the precipitation of VC accelerates with the decreasing temperature, as shown in  Fig. 9 (b).

Fig. 9 (c) and (d) illustrate the precipitation history of Nb and V in 22MnB5NbV during the hot stamping process. Nb almost precipitates completely during the austenitization process while V absolutely dissolves in the austenite phase and starts to precipitate as VC at 800 °C, indicating that the precipitation of V is later than Nb.  Fig. 9 (d) shows there is still 10% dissolved V in the form of a solution even at room temperature. The leaching experiment presents that 88% of Nb and 25% of V exist as precipitates in 22MnB5NbV. The precipitation of Nb estimated by JmatPro is consistent with that by the leaching experiment, but there is a little difference for V. The difference in the results of precipitated V between the JmatPro and the leaching experiment may result from the influence of precipitation kinetics.

The morphology of precipitate in 22MnB5NbV was characterized by TEM, as shown in  Fig. 10 
                         .  Fig. 10 (a) shows a cubic particle with a size of about 290 while most particles are spherical with a smaller size. It is composed of 53.73C-24.48Ti-20.44Nb-1.36Fe (in wt%) measured by energy dispersion spectroscopy (EDS). This particle is most possible precipitates at a high temperature, i.e., the cooling processes of continuous casting and hot-rolling. Besides, this particle intuitively precipitates at the prior austenite boundaries, which may have some pinning effect on grain growth during austenitizing, resulting in the refined microstructure in 22MnB5NbV.  Fig. 10 (b) and (c) present that there are many particles with compound composition precipitating at the boundaries.  Fig. 10 (e) presents the spherical particles with a much smaller size (< 20 nm) observed in the Fe matrix but not at the boundary. The austenite–martensite transformation is a non-diffusive process and the transformation time is short, resulting in negative kinetics condition of precipitation  [48,49] . So, the particles with a size smaller than 20 nm are very likely to precipitate during the hot coiling process. Moreover, these particles are the compound-composition carbides of (Nb, Ti, V)C, in which Nb accounts for the largest proportion. Specifically, the Nb, Ti, and V account for 25%, 11%, and 4% (in wt%) on average, respectively, according to the EDS analysis results listed in  Table 3 
                         .  Fig. 10 (d) also shows that the spectral signal for element Nb is strongest while that for element V is weakest. These suggest that Nb and Ti may precipitate first and be the heterogeneous nucleation site for V precipitation, which is consistent with the theoretical calculation results in  Fig. 9 . The above results suggest that most Nb exists in the form of precipitates but V is not although the addition amount is the same, inferring that the microalloying effect of Nb may be better than that of V in terms of improving HE by nano-precipitates which are irreversible hydrogen trapping sites. In addition, the TEM-SAD (selected area diffraction) indicates that there is a coherent interface that satisfies the Baker-Nutting orientation relationship between the nanoscale precipitate (carbide) and the Fe matrix, as shown in  Fig. 10 (f). This orientation relationship was also confirmed by previous studies  [50] . The lattice parameter of the carbide estimated by the TEM-SAD is 0.4331 nm, which is in the range of  a 
                         NbC  = 0.4507 nm,  a 
                         TiC  = 0.4336 nm, and  a 
                         VC  = 0.4160 nm  [51] , illustrating that the carbide is a compound of (Nb, Ti, V)C.

The nanoscale carbide has a strong interaction with the hydrogen atom, which is regarded as an irreversible hydrogen trapping in steel  [7,27] . Wei et al.  [29]  pointed out that the size and the coherency of the carbide precipitated in the matrix have a significant effect on the anti-HE property, and the coherent or semicoherent carbide usually has a greater capacity for hydrogen absorption than the incoherent carbide. The coherency is intrinsically related to the size of the carbide, and the carbide with a large size would break the coherency due to the existence of stress surrounding the interface of carbide/matrix. Studies pointed out that the carbide with a size smaller than 10 nm was assumed to play an important role in hydrogen trapping  [52] .

To evaluate the size distribution of the nanoscale precipitates, 189 and 564 particles in the 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV are observed, respectively.  Fig. 11 
                          presents the size distribution of the precipitates in 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV. The proportion of the particles with a size smaller than 10 nm is about 81% and 97% for 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, respectively. The average size of the nanoscale precipitates in 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV are 8.7 nm and 4.9 nm, respectively. The volume fraction of the nanoscale precipitates in the 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV are estimated by the McCall-Boyd method  [36,53] , which are 0.053 vol% and 0.082 vol%, respectively. There are more dispersed and finer nanoscale carbides in 22MnB5NbV due to the Nb-V microalloying, resulting in the enhanced capacity of hydrogen trapping. This is why the non-diffusible hydrogen amount in the 22MnB5NbV is greater than that in the 22MnB5, as shown in  Fig. 2  (the 2nd peak at 350–550 °C).

sections.heading: Reversible and irreversible hydrogen trapping sites
paragraphs: Usually, the desorption activation energy smaller than 30 kJ/mol is categorized as reversible hydrogen trapping, such as grain boundary (17 kJ/mol) and dislocation (20–26 kJ/mol)  [45,54] . In the present study, the refined microstructure is an important factor attributed to the satisfactory resistance to HE for 22MnB5NbV, because the grain boundary is in favor of hydrogen trapping  [37,46] . There is more dispersive and fine carbonitride in the 22MnB5NbV due to the addition of Nb-V, which has a refining effect on the microstructure. As a result, the PAGS and martensite lath width in the 22MnB5NbV respectively decreased from 11.3 to 8.1 μm and from 0.35 to 0.15 μm, compared with the 22MnB5. Stopher et al.  [55]  pointed out that the fine grains (< 10 μm) were dramatically beneficial to the capacity of hydrogen trapping for pure iron systems. So, the finer microstructure with more grain boundary plays a considerable role in the improving effect of anti-HE in 22MnB5NbV.

The nanoscale carbide has a strong interaction with hydrogen atoms, which is taken as an irreversible hydrogen trapping site in steel  [7,27] . Usually, there is a significant difference in the capacity of hydrogen adsorption between the (semi)coherent and incoherent interface of carbonitride/matrix  [30,44,56,57] . Although the C vacancies inside the incoherent NbC, TiC, and VC are effective hydrogen traps, the hydrogen atom is difficult to diffuse from the matrix to the C vacancies of carbides [25,29] . Thus, the incoherent carbide is usually invalid or negligible in hydrogen trapping  [30] . The hydrogen is inclined to be trapped rather at the (semi)coherent interface of carbide/matrix than inside the carbide, which should be induced by the stress field originating from the semicoherent or coherent precipitation. This is confirmed for the TiC  [58,59] , VC  [46,60] , and NbC  [29,30] . Pressouyre  [56]  pointed out that the stress field in the matrix surrounding the coherent precipitate played an important role in hydrogen trapping. Steiner et al.  [61]  further suggested the stress field had a significant effect on solute diffusion. In general, the stress field surrounding the (semi)coherent interface of precipitate/matrix increases with the precipitated size  [62] . But the (semi)coherent interface would transform into incoherent to release the strain by forming dislocation on the surface of the precipitate once the precipitate grows into a critical size  [58,59] . Based on previous studies, the critical size of the (semi)coherent or incoherent carbonitride of Ti, V, and Nb, which could be taken as an effective hydrogen trap, is generally smaller than 10 nm  [52,63] , and the coarsening precipitate usually fails to trap hydrogen  [59] . In the present study, the precipitates with a size smaller than 10 nm, which may be a (semi)coherent interface and effective hydrogen trap, account for 81% and 97% in the 22MnB5 and 22MnB5NbV, respectively. That is, there are more (semi)coherent precipitates in the 22MnB5NbV, which contribute to the improvement in anti-HE. Here we will discuss the effect of the strain field surrounding the nanoscale precipitate on the diffusion and accumulation of hydrogen atoms.

Thus, the content of diffusive hydrogen atoms in the matrix decreases, resulting in an improvement in resisting HE. The strain field induced by the NbC is greater than that by the TiC or VC, which means more hydrogen atoms could be gathered at the coherent interface of Fe/NbC in comparison with Fe/TiC or Fe/VC. Not only NbC but also more nanoscale coherent carbides in 22MnB5NbV, resulting in the performance in resisting HE for 22MnB5NbV being better than that for 22MnB5.

sections.heading: Effect of Nb-V combined  microalloying  on HE
paragraphs: The positive effect of the combined addition of Nb-V on anti-HE for PHS has been proved in the present study. The previous studies  [31,40,42]  also confirmed that the combined addition of Nb-V in steel could get better performance in some respects than the sole addition of Nb or V, resulting from the difference in the size, distribution, and type of precipitates, as well as the microstructure. Theoretically, with the decreasing temperature during the process of solidification and/or heat treatment, the precipitation sequence of the carbonitride is Ti > Nb > V under the same condition  [69] . For the sole addition of Ti, Nb, or V, Ti and Nb partially precipitate as a coarsened carbonitride at a high temperature and fail to keep interface coherency while the V only partially precipitates as VC at a slightly lower temperature  [70] , which is difficult to achieve the best effect on resisting HE  [30,60] . But for the combined addition of Ti, Nb, and V, the Ti, Nb, and V can be infinitely interchangeable in the carbonitride due to the crystal structure of the carbonitride of Ti, Nb, and V are similar  [71] , resulting in the precipitation of fine and dispersed compound-composition carbonitride  [72] , as shown in  Fig. 10 .

To clarify the spatial structure of the nanoscale precipitate, a carbide with a size of about 7 nm in 22MnB5NbV was identified using APT, as shown in  Fig. 12 
                         . It is particularly noteworthy that the carbide has a compound composition of (Nb, V)C, in which V is located at the outer layer while Nb is the matrix, indicating that the element of Nb precipitates first and V precipitates later in 22MnB5NbV. This is corresponding to the results of the thermodynamic calculation and leaching experiment.  Fig. 12 (c) presents that the averaged concentrations of Nb, V, and C in the carbide are around 39.38, 3.67, and 44.08 at.%, respectively. The balanced content maybe 12.87 at.% Ti. The composition of this carbide is similar to those in  Table 3 . Moreover, the hydrogen trapping effect of the compound composition carbide was verified using the APT, as shown in  Fig. 12 . The hydrogens are mainly trapped on the interface between the (Nb, V)C and Fe matrix.

The precipitation with a compound composition can improve the lattice misfit between the carbonitride and Fe matrix  [50,64] , which can promote the (semi)coherent precipitate with a larger size and greater strain field, resulting in an enhanced capacity of hydrogen trapping. In addition, the addition of V in (Nb, V)C can reduce the interface energy of the carbides that precipitate in the Fe matrix  [70] , which is conducive to the precipitation of dispersed and fine carbides (that is, more hydrogen traps), as shown in  Fig. 11 . On the other hand, the refined microstructure resulting from the pinning effect of precipitates can also play an important role in hydrogen trapping and hindering hydrogen induced crack propagation. Thus, the combined addition of alloying elements in PHS usually presents a better performance in anti-HE than the sole addition.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: A novel press-hardened steel (22MnB5NbV), which was microalloyed with 0.04Nb-0.04 V (in wt%) based on traditional 22MnB5, was developed to improve the hydrogen embrittlement. The duration of no cracking in the 0.5 mol/L hydrochloric acid solution is > 300 h for 22MnB5NbV even though the pre-bending stress is close to the ultimate tensile strength of 1500–1600 MPa, but that is only 12 h for 22MnB5. The fracture morphology of the SSRT specimen with H-charging shows tiny dimples for 22MnB5NbV while that shows a quasi-cleavage feature with secondary cracks for 22MnB5, illustrating that the 22MnB5NbV has better toughness than 22MnB5 despite the existence of hydrogen. The capacity of hydrogen trapping for 22MnB5NbV is 2.09 times that for 22MnB5, according to the hydrogen desorption peak at 100–300 °C of TDS. This is mainly due to the refinement of martensite lath, which decreases from 0.35 to 0.15 μm. The proportion of the precipitates with a size smaller than 10 nm increases from 81% to 97% because of the combined addition of Nb-V, enhancing the capacity of irreversible hydrogen traps for 22MnB5NbV. The precipitates in 22MnB5NbV are almost complex carbides of (Nb, Ti, V)C. In particular, the nanoscale (Nb, Ti, V)C, in which V is located at the outer layer while Nb is the matrix, is identified using APT. This illustrates that the V-bearing carbides precipitate later and take the Nb-bearing carbides as the heterogeneous nucleation sites. APT verifies that the hydrogen is mainly trapped on the interface between the (Nb, V)C and Fe matrix. Although the initial addition amount is the same, the Nb and V exist in the form of precipitates are 88% and 25% in 22MnB5NbV, respectively, inferring that the microalloying effect of Nb may be more efficient than that of V in terms of improving HE by nano-precipitates which are irreversible hydrogen traps.
